I'm Swiss, maybe I can shed a light on a few of these things "we" percieve as normal (Of course, these things are not followed by each and very individual, we have hams and REEE too.):

After returning from the trip, I've been trying to figure out why it is that Americans are so much fatter. It's not that the food in Europe is vastly different than that in America.

A considerable part of Europe has very strong food culture (Spain, France, Greece and Italy are the most widely-known ones but we have a lot of different, regional cuisines and people are proud of that) and fast food (McDonalds and comparable stuff) is actually looked down upon because of all the litter it produces and how much worse it is in comparison. Also (and this is more about the mediterranean cuisines than about the "heavier" German/Austrian ones): it's light food. Lots of grilled meat or fish, salads with little dressing, lots of vegetables and so on, little gravy or ketchup/mayo.

The typical "3 meals a day, either lunch or dinner is reserved as family time" structure is much more established, too.

Additionally, there's a strong tourism industry over here (especially around the alps) so a lot of people naturally come in contact with all sorts of different cuisines - and those people are way more likely to dislike the good ole triple McBeetus because it's just not as tasty in comparison.

We also don't have things such as your student loans (though tuition fees are much lower because it's subsidised by the gvt), so students are chronically short on money. One way to save money is to do your grocery shopping right before the store closes as they usually offer substantial discount on vegetables, fruit, opened meat and so on. That means you sometimes get a bunch of random items and have to somehow make a meal out of that so naturally, people will have to learn how to cook least to some degree. Adding to that is the price of fast food. McD is expensive as fuck over here (we're talking 6+ bucks for a BigMac and 10+ if you want some soda with it) so students literally can't afford to frequent such restaurants.

Right now I'm in England taking English classes (yay, being fluent is not enough, I need a Cambridge degree to be eligible for university...) and you see a surprising amount of restaurants where you can get a full dinner for 20ish pounds. You don't have that on continental Europe. When you eat out, prepare to spend at least 75 bucks, 100< if you want to drink wine. Since large parts of our country are catering towards tourism at least to some degree, you get these inflated rip-off prices everywhere. Shit's expensive yo.

In fact, I'd say the food here is even more fattening than the food in America. When I go to the grocery store here, whole aisles are dedicated to chocolate, chips, cured meats, cookies, and cheese. In fact, I have yet to see all the diet food that is prevalent in America (I'm looking at you, fat-free everything). There are shops everywhere selling deep fried sausages, croquettes, fries, kapsalon (fries topped with cheese & meat and drowned in garlic mayo), you name it. One of the most popular dipping sauces in the country is basically mayo.

You can get anything here. I mean literally anything, like in the US. People just eat less of it for the aforementioned reasons. Once you leave the tourist/crowded areas, you'll find that the popularity of fast food drops fairly quickly.

As for the diet food: it exists but is often frowned upon as "bastardised real food". I've tried it a few times, it actually does taste like shit.

Yet, the people here are not nearly as fat as those in America. I'd say that the difference is that while the food consumed here may be similar to that in America, there is a prevalence of controlled eating. Instead of gorging themselves at every meal, most of my European friends only eat till they are full and hit the gym every day.

One advantage of governmental healthcare plans (actual ones, going way beyond Obamacare) help a great deal with that. I, for example, can send the bill for my gym membership to my insurance and get 250 bucks back every year. Can't complain about a 12 month membership for the price of a dinner out.
